opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting problem, and I think it's one that a lot of people in the community are wrestling with right now. The core issue is that with a model like GPT-4, we don't have access to the things we'd normally want as scientists. We don't know exactly what the training data was, we don't know the full details of the architecture or the training procedure, and the model itself can change underneath you over time as it gets updated behind an API. So when you run an evaluation and see some behavior, it's hard to say why it's happening, or even whether you'd see the same thing next month.

One big piece of this is contamination. If you're testing on a benchmark, you often can't rule out that the benchmark, or something very close to it, was in the training data. Then what looks like reasoning or generalization might partly be memorization, and you can't easily tell the two apart from the outside.

Another piece, and this is something we've spent time on, is that the conclusions you draw can depend a lot on how you measure. Some of the excitement around so-called emergent abilities, for example, where capabilities seem to suddenly appear at scale, can be at least partly explained by the choice of metric. If you use a harsh, discontinuous metric like exact match, you can get these sharp jumps, whereas a smoother metric often shows much more gradual, predictable improvement. So part of the scientific challenge is being careful that what we're seeing is a property of the model and not an artifact of our evaluation choices.

And then there's the broader question of what we're actually trying to measure. Things like trustworthiness, fairness, robustness, privacy, toxicity: these are multifaceted, and with a black-box system you're inferring them purely through inputs and outputs. That means you have to be really thoughtful about designing prompts and test cases, about reproducibility, and about being honest regarding the limits of what your evaluation can claim. I think the field is still building the measurement science to do that well, and that's a big part of what makes it exciting to work on.

r001.rationale: It says the model may be updated behind an API, making it hard to know whether an evaluation would produce the same result later.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core challenge is that we don't really have access to the thing we're studying. With GPT-4, and increasingly with a lot of these frontier models, you get an API. You don't know the training data, you don't know the exact architecture, you often don't even know if the model behind the endpoint is the same one you queried last week. And that creates a fundamental tension with how we normally think about science.

In most empirical science, reproducibility is kind of the bedrock. You run an experiment, someone else runs it, they should get the same result. But if I evaluate GPT-4 in March and you evaluate it in June and the model has been updated in between, we're not even talking about the same object anymore. So a lot of the claims that get made end up being, in a sense, claims about a snapshot that nobody can go back and verify.

The second piece is contamination. We have these benchmarks that we've all agreed are meaningful, and the honest answer is we don't know whether the model has seen them during training. When a model does really well on some test, is that capability, or is that memorization? And because the data is closed, you can't actually resolve that question. You end up doing these indirect things, like perturbing inputs or constructing fresh tasks, and those are useful, but they're workarounds for a problem we shouldn't have to have.

And then there's a third thing, which is a bit more subtle. A lot of what we care about with these models isn't a single number. It's things like, is it robust, is it fair, is it calibrated, does it behave differently under distribution shift, can it be jailbroken. Those are properties of the whole system, and they interact. So when we did the DecodingTrust work, one of the takeaways was that a model can look great on one axis and be pretty fragile on another, and you'd never see that if you only looked at the standard leaderboard numbers.

So I'd say the challenge isn't that evaluating black-box models is impossible. It's that we have to be much more careful about what claims we're actually licensed to make, we have to treat evaluations as having a shelf life, and honestly as a community we need to push for enough transparency that the scientific questions are even answerable in the first place.

r001.rationale: It says the model behind an API may change between queries, so evaluations at different times may concern different versions of the model.

astra-6.text:
The big challenge is that we don’t know exactly what we’re evaluating. We can query the model and measure its behavior, but we don’t know what data it was trained on or all the steps that went into building it. So if it does well on a benchmark, is that evidence that it generalizes, or has it seen those examples before? It’s difficult to distinguish those explanations.

And the model can change behind the API. If I run an experiment today and you run the same experiment later, we may not actually be testing the same system. That makes reproducibility difficult. We can still learn useful things from these evaluations, but we have to be careful about how broadly we interpret the results.

r001.rationale: The response says a model can change behind the API, so repeating an experiment later may test a different system and undermine reproducibility.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the big challenges is that we don’t know exactly what’s in the training data. So when we evaluate a model on a benchmark, it can be difficult to tell whether we’re measuring its ability to generalize or whether it has already seen those examples. And that’s not necessarily something you can resolve just by querying the model.

There’s also the question of reproducibility. If the model behind an API changes, you might run the same experiment later and get a different result. So we can study the behavior of the system we have access to, but it’s much harder to make strong scientific claims about why it behaves that way or whether those findings will hold across versions.

r001.rationale: The response says the model behind an API may change, causing the same experiment to produce different results later, which identifies ongoing model changes as an evaluation challenge.
